fields.title: Elisabeth Elliot (For Teens)
fields.description: In January 1956 Elisabeth Elliot's husband Jim and four other young missionaries were speared to death on a sandbar in the Ecuadorian rainforest. Less than three years later she walked into the forest with her three-year-old daughter to live among the men who had killed him. She had already lost a murdered language helper and a stolen suitcase of work; she would go on to nurse a second husband through cancer, write books that reached millions, and spend her last years silenced by dementia. This teen edition tells her whole life straight, including the failures, the quarrels and the story she spent decades correcting.

qa.question: Who was Elisabeth Elliot?
qa.answer: An American missionary linguist and writer, born in Brussels in 1926 and raised in a devout Philadelphia family. She worked in Ecuador from 1952 to 1963, lost her first husband Jim when the Waorani killed him and four other missionaries in 1956, then lived among the Waorani herself. Back in America she became one of the best-known Christian authors and radio speakers of her time. She died in 2015.

qa.question: Is the book honest about the hard parts?
qa.answer: Yes. It tells of the death of a woman she tried to help, the murder of her language helper, the killings of 1956, her conflict with Rachel Saint, her own bluntness, the debate over her teaching on women, the hard side of her third marriage as her biographer describes it, and her long years of dementia.

qa.question: What does “Doe the nexte thynge” mean?
qa.answer: It is the refrain of an old anonymous poem that Elisabeth Elliot quoted throughout her life. It means that when you can't see the whole road, you don't have to. You only have to do, in faith, the duty in front of you, and leave the rest to God.

qa.question: Did the Waorani all become Christians right after the five missionaries died?
qa.answer: No. Some of the men who took part in the killings did later become believers and leaders, but the change was slow and uneven, killing did not stop all at once, and other Waorani groups went on feuding for years. Elisabeth Elliot said so herself in a 1996 epilogue to her most famous book.

qa.question: How did she treat the people who killed her husband?
qa.answer: She went to live among them in 1958, learned their language and gave them medical care. She did not excuse what they had done, but she did not hate them, and she refused to describe them either as monsters or as noble innocents. They were people to her.

qa.question: Where do the stories come from?
qa.answer: From the full-length biography of Elisabeth Elliot, which draws on her own books, Jim Elliot's journals, her parents' published letters, the authorised biography by Ellen Vaughn and the work of historians such as Kathryn Long. Where the sources disagree, this edition says so. Her own writings are still in copyright, so her thoughts are told here in paraphrase.

qa.question: Why did she go to live among the Waorani?
qa.answer: They invited her, through Dayuma and two Waorani women, Mintaka and Mankamu, who had lived in her home. She was one of the few outsiders learning their language, and she believed God was calling her to make Christ known to them. She did not think being a mother released her from obeying, or that obeying guaranteed safety.

qa.question: What can a teenager today take from her story?
qa.answer: That you can trust God without getting explanations; that waiting and doing the next thing are real faithfulness; that honest questions belong in prayer; and that even heroes are cracked clay pots God chooses to work through.

fields.title: A Goodly Heritage
fields.body_html:
“The lines are fallen unto me in pleasant places; yea, I have a goodly heritage.” — Psalm 16:6 (KJV)

Elisabeth Howard was born on 21 December 1926 in Brussels, Belgium. She wasn't Belgian. Her parents, Philip and Katharine Howard, were American missionaries working with the Belgian Gospel Mission. While she was still a baby they went home to the United States, so she had no memory of the country she was born in. To her family and friends she was Betty, and Betty she stayed for most of her life. The world would come to know her as Elisabeth Elliot.

Her father joined the staff of the Sunday School Times, a weekly paper from Philadelphia that gave Bible lessons to Sunday school teachers all over America, and in time he became its editor. Her great-grandfather had made it famous. So Betty grew up among people who wrote for a living, cared about words, and judged a sentence by whether it said exactly what it meant. The plain, precise way she wrote as an adult started in her father's office.

The family lived in Germantown, in Philadelphia, and from 1936 in Moorestown, New Jersey. There were six children: Philip, Betty, David, Ginny, Tom and Jim. These were the years of the Great Depression, and money was never plentiful. Nothing was wasted. Nobody complained about it; it was simply how things were done. That training in being content would serve her well in a forest clearing many years later.

Twice a day, every day, the family gathered for worship. They sang a hymn, all the verses, until the children knew scores of them by heart without trying. Their father read the Bible and prayed: for each child by name, for the country, and for missionaries all over the world, many of whom had sat at the Howards' own table. The children memorized Scripture. They were expected to obey the first time. Summers were spent in the mountains of New Hampshire, at Franconia, climbing hills, picking berries and learning the names of birds and trees. She loved it more than anywhere.

Betty grew up tall, quiet, bookish and painfully shy. She felt awkward and plain beside other girls. In 1941, at fourteen, she was sent to a Christian boarding school in Florida, the Hampden DuBose Academy. The headmistress, Mrs DuBose, was formidable, and she singled Betty out. She told her plainly that shyness was not a virtue to be indulged. It was a way of being wrapped up in yourself, and a Christian has a duty to look outward and put other people at ease. Betty was frightened of her. She also took her seriously. She learned to stand straight, look people in the eye, talk to strangers and speak in public. People later thought her calm was natural. It wasn't. It was learned, at some cost.

At evening chapel Mrs DuBose often read from Amy Carmichael, an Irish missionary in South India who had rescued children in danger. In her little book If, every entry ends with the same line: “then I know nothing of Calvary love.” Betty was captivated. She later called Amy Carmichael her first spiritual mother. By the time she graduated in 1944 she knew what she wanted to do with her life: translate the Bible into a language that had never had it.

Notice two things. First, a “goodly heritage” in the psalm is not the same as an easy one. Betty's family was strict, not rich, and not perfect, and its six children went in different directions. Her parents could not make their children believe. But they gave them the words, and in her case the words took root. Whatever your family gave you or didn't, God can still give you his words. Second, being shy is not a sin, but it can become a hiding place. Betty learned that looking outward is something you can practise.

One thing to do this week: pick one person you usually avoid because talking to them feels awkward, and ask them one real question about themselves. Then actually listen to the answer.

fields.title: The Shadow of a Cross
fields.body_html:
“I beseech you therefore, brethren, by the mercies of God, that ye present your bodies a living sacrifice, holy, acceptable unto God, which is your reasonable service.” — Romans 12:1 (KJV)

In the autumn of 1944 Betty Howard arrived at Wheaton College, near Chicago, to study classical Greek. It was an unusual choice for a young woman then, but she had a reason: if she was going to translate the Bible, she wanted to work from the original text of the New Testament. She read Homer and Plato as well as the Gospels, and she drilled grammar the old way. Greek suited her precise mind. Finding exactly the right word, and refusing to settle for a vague one, became a habit for life.

At Wheaton she was serious and rather solitary, more respected than popular. She prayed constantly about God's will. She had decided she would rather stay single and serve God on the mission field than marry the wrong man.

In 1945 a new student arrived from Portland, Oregon. Jim Elliot was a year younger than Betty: handsome, athletic, outspoken, funny and intense. He was on the wrestling team and the missionary fellowship, and he too studied Greek. He had little time for what he called frivolity, and he was deeply moved by the diary of David Brainerd, a young missionary who had died at twenty-nine. Jim's closest friend was Betty's brother Dave. At Christmas 1947 Dave brought Jim home to Moorestown. Jim joined the family prayers and hymn-singing and stayed up late talking. When the new term began in January 1948, he and Betty started studying Greek together. Both were good at it, and both were competitive.

By spring it was obvious to both of them that this was more than friendship, and neither knew what to do. Betty believed a woman should not show her feelings until a man had declared his. Jim had come to believe, from Paul's words in First Corinthians 7, that God might be calling him to stay single so he could go to hard, dangerous places without dividing his heart. He wasn't sure. And he wasn't willing to let his feelings decide for him.

On the evening of 9 June 1948, just before her graduation, they went for a walk south of the campus and came to a cemetery. There, for the first time, they told each other what they felt. Jim also told her that God might be leading him to stay single, and that he could promise her nothing. They agreed to give their love back to God. The picture they used was Abraham in Genesis 22, laying his son Isaac on the altar: a gift from God, precious, and for that very reason offered back to him with no conditions. As they sat there, the rising moon threw the shadow of a large stone cross between them. Neither treated it as a magic sign. But both remembered it as a picture of what they had just decided.

Then she graduated and left. There was no engagement and no promise. They would write, sometimes often, sometimes hardly at all. Her private journals, read long afterwards, show that she sometimes found the uncertainty almost unbearable. Years later she told the story in a book, Passion and Purity, which many young people found a lifeline. Others felt it turned one couple's unusual path into a rule for everyone. That criticism is worth hearing. Their exact path isn't a pattern you have to copy.

What is worth copying is the heart of it. Romans 12 doesn't describe one dramatic moment of giving something up. It describes a living sacrifice: something you keep offering, day after day. The full-length biography puts it well: the altar was not a moment, it was a place they had to keep coming back to. Maybe there is something you want so much that it's hard to pray honestly about it: a relationship, a place on a team, a dream. Trusting God with it doesn't mean pretending you don't care. It means caring, and still saying, “It's yours.”

One thing to do this week: write down the one thing you want most right now. Then pray about it honestly, telling God how much you want it and that you are putting it in his hands. Do it again tomorrow.

study_questions.answer: She believed God was calling her to translate the Bible, and she wanted to work from the original text of the New Testament.

study_questions.question: Why was Jim unwilling to make Betty any promise in 1948?
study_questions.answer: He thought God might be calling him to stay single for the sake of hard missionary work, and he would not let his feelings decide the question before he was sure.

study_questions.question: What does it mean that “the altar was not a moment”?
study_questions.answer: Giving their love back to God wasn't a single decision; they had to keep trusting God with it again and again through years of uncertainty.

fields.title: Waiting Well
fields.body_html:
“It is good that a man should both hope and quietly wait for the salvation of the LORD.” — Lamentations 3:26 (KJV)

In the autumn of 1948 Betty went north to the Prairie Bible Institute in Three Hills, Alberta, a farming town on the Canadian plains. Winter there is bitterly cold. The school was plain and strict, and its founder, L. E. Maxwell, preached about dying daily to self. Students rose early, worked hard and lived simply. Betty had laid her love on the altar and meant to leave it there. She was lonely and far from home. When Jim's letters came, they were careful and promised nothing. Afterwards she stayed on in Alberta for a while, teaching Sunday school among the farms around a hamlet called, of all things, Patience.

Jim finished at Wheaton in 1949 and went home to Portland, working, preaching in small churches and asking God where to go. In the summer of 1950 he attended a linguistics course in Oklahoma, run by Wycliffe Bible Translators, and there he heard about Ecuador: about the Quichua people of the eastern rainforest, and beyond them a people called the Waorani, whom no outsider had yet reached in friendship. Within months he was sure God was sending him there. A gifted young man from Seattle named Pete Fleming agreed to go with him, and on 4 February 1952 they sailed.

None of that made things simpler for Betty. Jim still wasn't sure about marriage, and he still said so. For a while he seemed to lean towards it, then away again. In four years after Wheaton they met only a handful of times, often briefly and sometimes painfully. Their letters, later published by their daughter, show two people who loved each other and were trying hard to be honest with God and each other, and who didn't always understand each other. There were misunderstandings and silences.

Meanwhile Betty kept preparing for her own calling. She took the same linguistics course, learning to analyse the sounds of an unwritten language, invent an alphabet for it, and build a grammar from nothing. She was good at it. Then she chose Ecuador, where there were peoples whose languages had never been written down.

Did she choose Ecuador because Jim was there? The biography is honest: the sources don't settle it, and maybe she couldn't have settled it herself. What is clear is that she went with no promise, no engagement and no understanding. She went to do her own work, as a single missionary. If Jim decided to stay single, she would be a single woman in Ecuador, and she knew it. She sailed in April 1952 and went up to Quito, the capital, high in the Andes, to learn Spanish. Jim was there. They saw each other. They still weren't engaged.

The years from 1948 to 1952 were some of the hardest of her life, not because something terrible happened, but because nothing did. She didn't know if she would marry the man she loved. She didn't know if her own calling would bear fruit. She just had to keep doing what was in front of her each day.

That might sound familiar. A lot of life as a teenager is waiting: for results, for a reply, for someone to notice you, for life to start. Lamentations was written by a man sitting in the ruins of his city. Right in the middle of his grief he says it is good to “hope and quietly wait.” Quiet waiting isn't doing nothing. It's refusing to grab what God hasn't given yet, and doing today's work well in the meantime. Betty learned it in these years, imperfectly and with plenty of tears. She would need it again.

One thing to do this week: think of one thing you are waiting on. Each time you catch yourself checking, refreshing or worrying about it this week, stop and do one useful job that belongs to today instead.

study_questions.question: Where did Betty go after Wheaton, and what was it like?
study_questions.answer: To the Prairie Bible Institute in Three Hills, Alberta: a cold, remote, strict Bible school where she studied, felt lonely, and received careful letters from Jim that promised nothing.

study_questions.question: Did Betty go to Ecuador engaged to Jim?
study_questions.answer: No. She went with no promise or understanding, to do her own language work as a single missionary, knowing she might stay single.

study_questions.question: What does the chapter say “quiet waiting” means?
study_questions.answer: Not doing nothing, but refusing to grab what God hasn't given yet and doing today's work faithfully in the meantime.

fields.title: These Strange Ashes
fields.body_html:
“For my thoughts are not your thoughts, neither are your ways my ways, saith the LORD. For as the heavens are higher than the earth, so are my ways higher than your ways, and my thoughts than your thoughts.” — Isaiah 55:8-9 (KJV)

By the autumn of 1952 Betty was on the far western slope of the Andes, below the clouds, in a belt of dense, wet forest. Near the frontier town of Santo Domingo was a scattering of clearings called San Miguel de los Colorados. The Spanish called the people there the Colorados, “the red ones,” because the men dyed their hair bright red with paste from the achiote seed. Their own name is Tsáchila. Their language had never been written down. Betty joined three other single women missionaries as the team's linguist. This was the work she had spent eight years preparing for.

There was no grammar, no dictionary, no teacher. She pointed at things and wrote down what people said. She listened to the same word again and again until she could hear its sounds, and filed everything on cards. It rained constantly. There were insects, snakes and mud. Most of the Colorados were polite but not interested. What she needed most was an informant: someone who spoke Colorado as a native and Spanish well enough to explain it.

Then came the first loss. A Colorado woman went into a hard labour, and Betty was there. She wasn't a nurse, and no doctor could be reached. What help could be given was given, and it wasn't enough. The woman died. Betty was shaken to the roots. She had come believing God would bless work done in obedience to him. She had obeyed, and a young mother was dead.

Then came the answer to her prayers. A man named Don Macario had grown up on a farm alongside Colorado children and spoke both languages with ease. He was a believer, intelligent and patient, and willing to help. Day after day they sat together. Words became lists, and lists became patterns. She began to see how an alphabet might work. It must have felt as if God was finally confirming her call.

Then Macario was killed. By the account usually given, he was clearing land he believed was his when some men arrived and claimed it, and when he wouldn't give way, he was shot dead. There was no one to replace him, and the work stopped. She had prayed for a helper, God had given one, and now he was gone in the most senseless way imaginable. If obedience didn't guarantee results, what did it guarantee?

In January 1953 she became engaged to Jim (that story is next) and had to leave for the other side of the Andes. She packed her notebooks, cards and charts into a suitcase to send to the colleagues who would carry on. As far as anyone knows, there were no copies. The suitcase was stolen from the back of a truck. Whoever took it found nothing of value to them. Nearly everything she had to show for her time among the Colorados was gone.

More than twenty years later she wrote about that year in a book called These Strange Ashes. The title came from a poem by Amy Carmichael about the ashes left after an offering has burned, and “this baffling sense of loss.” Betty didn't claim she had later found the hidden reasons. She decided the reasons were God's business. The question she had to answer wasn't “Why did God do this?” but “Will I keep trusting him without an explanation?”

Isaiah 55 isn't an explanation either. It's a reminder that God doesn't owe us one. Maybe you've done the right thing and watched it go wrong anyway. Faith that only works when things succeed isn't really faith yet. Betty learned that at twenty-six, earlier than most people do.

One thing to do this week: think of a time you did your best and it still fell apart. Tell God honestly what you don't understand about it. Don't force yourself to find a reason. Just ask him to help you keep trusting him anyway.

study_questions.question: What three losses did Betty suffer in her first year in Ecuador?
study_questions.answer: A Colorado woman she tried to help died in childbirth; her language helper Don Macario was shot dead in a land dispute; and the suitcase holding her language work was stolen.

study_questions.question: Where did the title *These Strange Ashes* come from?
study_questions.answer: From a poem by Amy Carmichael about the ashes left after an offering has burned, and “this baffling sense of loss.”

study_questions.question: What question did Betty decide she had to answer?
study_questions.answer: Not why God had allowed the losses, but whether she would go on trusting him without an explanation.

Their language had never been written down. Betty joined three other single women missionaries as the team's linguist. This was the work she had spent eight years preparing for. There was no grammar, no dictionary, no teacher. She pointed at things and wrote down what people said. She listened to the same word again and again until she could hear its sounds, and filed everything on cards. It rained constantly. There were insects, snakes and mud. Most of the Colorados were polite but not interested. What she needed most was an informant: someone who spoke Colorado as a native and Spanish well enough to explain it. Then came the first loss. A Colorado woman went into a hard labour, and Betty was there. She wasn't a nurse, and no doctor could be reached. What help could be given was given, and it wasn't enough. The woman died. Betty was shaken to the roots. She had come believing God would bless work done in obedience to him. She had obeyed, and a young mother was dead. Then came the answer to her prayers. A man named Don Macario had grown up on a farm alongside Colorado children and spoke both languages with ease. He was a believer, intelligent and patient, and willing to help. Day after day they sat together. Words became lists, and lists became patterns. She began to see how an alphabet might work. It must have felt as if God was finally confirming her call. Then Macario was killed. By the account usually given, he was clearing land he believed was his when some men arrived and claimed it, and when he wouldn't give way, he was shot dead. There was no one to replace him, and the work stopped. She had prayed for a helper, God had given one, and now he was gone in the most senseless way imaginable. If obedience didn't guarantee results, what did it guarantee? In January 1953 she became engaged to Jim (that story is next) and had to leave for the other side of the Andes. She packed her notebooks, cards and charts into a suitcase to send to the colleagues who would carry on. As far as anyone knows, there were no copies. The suitcase was stolen from the back of a truck. Whoever took it found nothing of value to them. Nearly everything she had to show for her time among the Colorados was gone. More than twenty years later she wrote about that year in a book called These Strange Ashes. The title came from a poem by Amy Carmichael about the ashes left after an offering has burned, and “this baffling sense of loss.” Betty didn't claim she had later found the hidden reasons. She decided the reasons were God's business. The question she had to answer wasn't “Why did God do this?” but “Will I keep trusting him without an explanation?” Isaiah 55 isn't an explanation either. It's a reminder that God doesn't owe us one. Maybe you've done the right thing and watched it go wrong anyway. Faith that only works when things succeed isn't really faith yet. Betty learned that at twenty-six, earlier than most people do. One thing to do this week: think of a time you did your best and it still fell apart. Tell God honestly what you don't understand about it. Don't force yourself to find a reason. Just ask him to help you keep trusting him anyway.

fields.title: Quichua First
fields.body_html:
“Two are better than one; because they have a good reward for their labour.” — Ecclesiastes 4:9 (KJV)

Late in January 1953 Jim came up from the eastern forest to Quito, and Betty came up from the western one. After five years of careful letters and long silences, Jim asked her to marry him. She said yes. Neither of them treated it as God's prize for waiting. It was a new step of obedience, and it came with a cost straight away.

Jim was committed to the Quichua people of the eastern rainforest, and he thought a wife who couldn't speak to them would be lonely and of little use to the work. So he made a condition: learn Quichua first, and then they would set a date. A man who had kept her waiting five years asked her to wait again. The full biography says fairly that this suited Jim's plans more than hers. It also says she agreed freely and never afterwards called it a grievance. She was a trained linguist; she knew how easily a missionary could live among people for years and understand little. If she was going to share the work, she wanted to share it properly.

She moved to a mission station called Dos Ríos and learned fast. That summer the river beside Jim's station at Shandia flooded and swept much of it away, so he was busy rebuilding. By autumn she knew enough Quichua to satisfy him.

They were married on 8 October 1953, Jim's twenty-sixth birthday, at the government registry office in Quito, in Spanish, as Ecuadorian law required. A handful of friends came. There was no church service, no procession, no reception. They weren't too poor for more; they both disliked show. Their families learned the news by letter. After a short honeymoon in Panama they headed into the forest.

Their first home was a tent. A Quichua headman named Atanasio at a place called Puyupungu had asked for a missionary and a school, so the newlyweds lived under canvas while a simple building went up, cooking over a fire among relentless insects. They seem to have enjoyed it. In 1954 they moved back to the rebuilt station at Shandia, into a house Jim built. Jim spoke Quichua by ear, easily and warmly, and preached. Betty heard the patterns underneath, and she could write the language down and teach others to read it. He was the preacher; she was the one with the notebook. On 27 February 1955 their daughter Valerie was born.

Later in life Elisabeth firmly discouraged people from imagining a perfect marriage. They had twenty-seven months together. By her own account they were happy months, and ordinary ones too, full of the small irritations of two strong-willed people sharing one small house.

From his first months in Ecuador, Jim had heard about another people, living between the Napo and Curaray rivers. They had killed outsiders who came into their land, and they killed one another in long-running feuds. Outsiders used a Quichua word for them meaning “savages.” Their own name is Waorani: “the people.” Jim longed to reach them. Betty knew the risks and didn't pretend she found them easy. But she didn't try to talk him out of it. In September 1955 two of Jim's friends, flying over the forest, finally spotted a cluster of Waorani houses.

Ecclesiastes is an unromantic book, but it makes an exception for teamwork: two are better than one. Love and obedience weren't opposites for Jim and Betty. Their marriage was a real love match and a real working partnership, and that doesn't only apply to marriage. God puts people with different gifts side by side on purpose.

One thing to do this week: think of someone whose gifts are different from yours, a sibling, a teammate or a friend. Tell them specifically one thing they do well that you couldn't do.

study_questions.answer: That Betty learn Quichua before they set a wedding date, so she could share the work with the Quichua people.

study_questions.question: Why was their wedding so simple?
study_questions.answer: Not because they were poor, but because both of them disliked show. It was a civil ceremony at the registry office in Quito, as Ecuadorian law required.

study_questions.question: How did Jim's and Betty's gifts fit together?
study_questions.answer: Jim spoke Quichua easily by ear and preached; Betty, the trained linguist, could analyse the language, write it down and teach others to read it.

fields.title: Palm Beach
fields.body_html:
“Verily, verily, I say unto you, Except a corn of wheat fall into the ground and die, it abideth alone: but if it die, it bringeth forth much fruit.” — John 12:24 (KJV)

Five men took part. Jim Elliot and Pete Fleming worked among the Quichua. Ed McCully lived at Arajuno, the station nearest Waorani country. Roger Youderian, a former army paratrooper, worked with the Shuar people. Nate Saint was the mission pilot who flew for them all. Every one of them was married, and four had young children. They called their plan Operation Auca, using the insulting word for the Waorani that most outsiders knew, a word the Waorani have rightly resented.

From October 1955 Nate flew in tight circles over the Waorani houses, lowering a bucket on a long line so it hung almost still. Week after week the men let down machetes, cooking pots, cloth and beads, and shouted friendly phrases through a loudspeaker. Jim had learned the phrases from Dayuma, a young Waorani woman who had fled her people years before; it later turned out he had learned them imperfectly. After a while the Waorani began tying gifts of their own to the line. To the men it looked like friendship. They kept the plan almost completely secret, afraid that publicity would wreck it. Their wives knew. Most colleagues didn't. Historians have since questioned both the secrecy and the speed.

On 3 January 1956 Nate landed on a sandbar on the Curaray River. The men built a shelter in a tree and called the place Palm Beach. On Friday 6 January three Waorani came out of the forest and waded across: a young man, Nenkiwi; a young woman, Gimari; and an older woman, Mintaka, who matters later in this story. They spent most of the day there. Nenkiwi even went up in the plane. The men were elated. Saturday, no one came.

On Sunday 8 January Nate saw what looked like a group of men walking towards the beach. Shortly after noon he radioed his wife Marj and promised to call again at half past four. At half past four the radio was silent. It never spoke again.

What happened was pieced together years later from Waorani who were there, and the accounts don't agree on every detail. Nenkiwi had gone off with Gimari without the older woman who should have gone with them, and to turn anger away from himself he told his relatives that the foreigners had attacked them. The Waorani already believed outsiders were dangerous; some believed they ate people. A group of men, led by an older warrior named Gikita, decided to kill them. While women showed themselves across the river to draw the missionaries' attention, the men attacked with spears. The five had guns, but they had agreed beforehand not to use them against the Waorani. Most accounts say shots were fired into the air. Nate's watch was later found stopped just after three o'clock. All five men died.

Six years earlier, on 28 October 1949, Jim had written in his journal: “He is no fool who gives what he cannot keep to gain what he cannot lose.” It is now one of the most quoted sentences in missionary history. But he wrote it as a young man testing his own heart, not as an epitaph. On the sandbar he didn't expect to die. The five went in hope, not looking for martyrdom. The sentence isn't a plan for dying. It's a decision about what to hold loosely.

This is a hard chapter, and it's worth holding two things together. These men were brave, and they refused to kill even to save themselves. They also made decisions that people who loved them have questioned. And the Waorani weren't monsters. They were frightened people acting on a lie and a long habit of violence. Real stories are like that. Jesus said a grain of wheat has to fall into the ground and die before it bears fruit. That evening, by the silent radios, nobody could see any fruit at all.

One thing to do this week: read Jim's sentence again and ask yourself honestly: what am I gripping that I can't keep anyway? Your free time, your image, your phone? Choose one way to loosen your grip on it this week for God's sake.

study_questions.question: Why did the five men keep their plan almost secret?
study_questions.answer: They feared that publicity would bring the government, the press or others into Waorani country and ruin any chance of peaceful contact.

study_questions.question: Why did the Waorani men decide to attack?
study_questions.answer: Nenkiwi, to deflect anger from himself, told them the foreigners had attacked; they already believed outsiders were dangerous, and some thought they ate people.

study_questions.question: What did Jim's 1949 sentence mean, according to this chapter?
study_questions.answer: It wasn't a plan for dying but a settled choice to hold loosely the things he couldn't keep anyway, in order to gain what he could never lose.

fields.title: The Next Thing
fields.body_html:
“A father of the fatherless, and a judge of the widows, is God in his holy habitation.” — Psalm 68:5 (KJV)

On Sunday evening the silent radio could still be explained. By Monday morning it couldn't. Another pilot, Johnny Keenan, flew over the Curaray and saw the little yellow plane on the sandbar with its fabric torn away. There was no sign of the men. The five wives gathered at the mission base at Shell Mera to wait.

A search party set out overland: missionaries, Quichua men and Ecuadorian soldiers. The US military sent aircraft and helicopters. During the week four of the men's bodies were found in the river and identified by their watches and wedding rings. A fifth, almost certainly Ed McCully's, had been seen by Quichua men further downstream but could not be recovered. In a violent rainstorm, the searchers buried the four together beside the beach and left in a hurry, afraid of being attacked. A photographer from Life magazine went with them, and his pictures of the widows and their children made their faces famous around the world.

People who were there were astonished at how calm the wives were. That calm was real, and it came from real faith. But it was later turned into something it wasn't: a picture of women who didn't grieve, or grieved less because they believed more. Elisabeth spent years correcting that. She did grieve, deeply and for a long time. She knew loneliness, exhaustion and fear. She had questions that weren't answered. What she didn't do was decide that God had failed her. Her calm wasn't the absence of grief. It was a decision about where to take it.

She was twenty-nine. Valerie was ten months old. She had no husband, no fixed income, and nothing to keep her in Ecuador. Most people expected her to go home.

She went back to Shandia. She took Valerie back to the house Jim had built and picked up his work: teaching, medical care, the young Quichua believers. She didn't see it as heroic. The work was there, the people were there, she spoke their language, and nobody else could do it. It was simply the obvious next thing. For the rest of her life she loved an old anonymous poem whose refrain, in its quaint old spelling, was “Doe the nexte thynge.” You don't have to see the whole road. You don't have to understand your grief before you get up in the morning. You only have to do what's in front of you. The other widows chose differently, and she never suggested hers was the only faithful choice.

Letters poured in from strangers. Many said they had given their lives to God because of the story. And she was asked to write it herself. In the first months of widowhood she read page after page of her husband's private journals and rebuilt, hour by hour, the weeks that had ended in his death. The book, Through Gates of Splendor, came out in 1957, named after a line in a hymn the men had sung before they left. It was plain and restrained. It didn't preach, and it didn't claim to know why God had allowed it. It has never gone out of print, and thousands of people said it led them to serve God. A year later she published Jim's life, and she let his journals stand as he wrote them, earnest and sometimes immature, rather than polishing him into a saint.

If you have lost someone, don't let anyone tell you that strong Christians don't grieve. Psalm 68 says God is a father to the fatherless and a defender of widows. He kept that promise to Elisabeth, not by taking the loss away, but by being with her in it while she did the next thing. If grief or heaviness is crushing you and won't lift, tell a safe person: a parent, a pastor, a teacher, a doctor, or a crisis line where you live.

One thing to do this week: the next time you feel overwhelmed, don't try to fix everything. Write down only the very next thing you need to do, do it, and then write down the one after that.

study_questions.answer: Plainly and with restraint. She didn't preach or claim to know why God allowed it, and she let Jim's journals stand without polishing him into a saint.

fields.title: Two Women from the Forest
fields.body_html:
“And I will bring the blind by a way that they knew not; I will lead them in paths that they have not known: I will make darkness light before them, and crooked things straight. These things will I do unto them, and not forsake them.” — Isaiah 42:16 (KJV)

When the way to the Waorani finally opened, it didn't come through any missionary plan. It came through three Waorani women.

The first was Dayuma. Years before Palm Beach, after members of her family were killed in the feuding, she had fled the forest. She ended up working on a farm in the foothills in conditions close to slavery, cut off from her people and sure she could never safely go back. Nate Saint's sister Rachel, a missionary with Wycliffe Bible Translators, had been living there, learning the Waorani language from her. In 1957 Rachel took Dayuma to the United States, where they appeared on national television and at Billy Graham's huge meeting in New York. Dayuma professed faith in Christ. For many American Christians she became living proof that the story would have a happy ending. The attention was intense, and some who knew both women later wondered whether it had been good for either of them.

Elisabeth had nothing to do with any of that. In November 1957 she was at Arajuno when two Quichua men arrived with startling news: two Waorani women had walked out of the forest and were at their house. She went at once.

Their names were Mankamu and Mintaka. They were older women, by most accounts relatives of Dayuma, and nobody outside ever fully understood why they came. Some said they wanted to know what had happened to Dayuma, and that the killing among their own people had made them willing to risk the outside world. And Mintaka was the older woman who had stood on the sandbar on 6 January 1956 with the five men, on the last Friday of their lives.

Elisabeth took them home to Shandia. For about ten months the two women lived with her and Valerie. She gave them food, shelter and care. Without quite meaning to, they gave her what she needed most: their language. It was the hardest language task of her life. Waorani is unrelated to any other known language. There was no grammar, no dictionary, and the two women had never been asked to explain their language to anyone. Day after day she listened, wrote and guessed, and was reminded how little she knew.

To her they weren't specimens to study or converts waiting to happen. They were people, with their own humour, sorrows and opinions. Later, her writing about the Waorani refused both to make them noble innocents and to make them monsters. She had learned that partly by living with Mintaka and Mankamu.

In 1958 Rachel and Dayuma came back to Ecuador, and Dayuma met the first people from her own tribe she had seen in more than ten years. On 3 September 1958, by the date usually given, Dayuma, Mintaka and Mankamu walked into the forest together. Nobody knew if they would come back. About three weeks later they did, with a party of Waorani men and women. Dayuma's people were alive. They had listened. And they had sent an invitation: Elisabeth and Rachel could come and live with them.

What Jim and his friends had prayed for came in a way none of them could have planned: not a plane and a loudspeaker, but a widow who opened her home and an exile who went home with news. Isaiah says God leads people “by a way that they knew not.” No one in this chapter could see far ahead. But their paths met.

Sometimes God's biggest doors open through the most ordinary kindness: a meal, a spare room, patience with someone who doesn't speak your language. The stranger at your door might be part of the story God is writing.

One thing to do this week: find someone who is new or on the outside, at school, at church or in your neighbourhood. Learn to say their name properly and spend real time with them, not as a project but as a person.

study_questions.question: Who were Mintaka and Mankamu?
study_questions.answer: Two older Waorani women who walked out of the forest in 1957. Mintaka had been on the sandbar with the five missionaries on 6 January 1956.

study_questions.question: How did Elisabeth learn the Waorani language?
study_questions.answer: By having Mintaka and Mankamu live with her for about ten months, listening and writing down what they said, in a language unrelated to any other known one.

study_questions.question: How did the invitation to live among the Waorani come?
study_questions.answer: Dayuma, Mintaka and Mankamu went back into the forest in September 1958 and returned about three weeks later with Waorani who invited Elisabeth and Rachel to come and live with them.

fields.body_text: “And I will bring the blind by a way that they knew not; I will lead them in paths that they have not known: I will make darkness light before them, and crooked things straight. These things will I do unto them, and not forsake them.” — Isaiah 42:16 (KJV) When the way to the Waorani finally opened, it didn't come through any missionary plan. It came through three Waorani women. The first was Dayuma. Years before Palm Beach, after members of her family were killed in the feuding, she had fled the forest. She ended up working on a farm in the foothills in conditions close to slavery, cut off from her people and sure she could never safely go back. Nate Saint's sister Rachel, a missionary with Wycliffe Bible Translators, had been living there, learning the Waorani language from her. In 1957 Rachel took Dayuma to the United States, where they appeared on national television and at Billy Graham's huge meeting in New York. Dayuma professed faith in Christ. For many American Christians she became living proof that the story would have a happy ending. The attention was intense, and some who knew both women later wondered whether it had been good for either of them. Elisabeth had nothing to do with any of that. In November 1957 she was at Arajuno when two Quichua men arrived with startling news: two Waorani women had walked out of the forest and were at their house. She went at once. Their names were Mankamu and Mintaka. They were older women, by most accounts relatives of Dayuma, and nobody outside ever fully understood why they came. Some said they wanted to know what had happened to Dayuma, and that the killing among their own people had made them willing to risk the outside world. And Mintaka was the older woman who had stood on the sandbar on 6 January 1956 with the five men, on the last Friday of their lives. Elisabeth took them home to Shandia. For about ten months the two women lived with her and Valerie. She gave them food, shelter and care. Without quite meaning to, they gave her what she needed most: their language. It was the hardest language task of her life. Waorani is unrelated to any other known language. There was no grammar, no dictionary, and the two women had never been asked to explain their language to anyone. Day after day she listened, wrote and guessed, and was reminded how little she knew. To her they weren't specimens to study or converts waiting to happen. They were people, with their own humour, sorrows and opinions. Later, her writing about the Waorani refused both to make them noble innocents and to make them monsters. She had learned that partly by living with Mintaka and Mankamu. In 1958 Rachel and Dayuma came back to Ecuador, and Dayuma met the first people from her own tribe she had seen in more than ten years. On 3 September 1958, by the date usually given, Dayuma, Mintaka and Mankamu walked into the forest together. Nobody knew if they would come back. About three weeks later they did, with a party of Waorani men and women. Dayuma's people were alive. They had listened. And they had sent an invitation: Elisabeth and Rachel could come and live with them. What Jim and his friends had prayed for came in a way none of them could have planned: not a plane and a loudspeaker, but a widow who opened her home and an exile who went home with news. Isaiah says God leads people “by a way that they knew not.” No one in this chapter could see far ahead. But their paths met. Sometimes God's biggest doors open through the most ordinary kindness: a meal, a spare room, patience with someone who doesn't speak your language. The stranger at your door might be part of the story God is writing. One thing to do this week: find someone who is new or on the outside, at school, at church or in your neighbourhood. Learn to say their name properly and spend real time with them, not as a project but as a person.

fields.title: She Went In
fields.body_html:
“Be not overcome of evil, but overcome evil with good.” — Romans 12:21 (KJV)

Not everyone thought she should go. To many of her friends and family it looked reckless to the point of foolishness: a young widow taking a three-year-old to live among the people who had speared her husband less than three years before. The Waorani had killed outsiders for generations and each other even more often. Nobody could promise the invitation was meant by everyone. If Elisabeth were killed, Valerie would be an orphan. If Valerie were killed, it was hard to imagine what anyone could say.

Elisabeth weighed all of it. She didn't wave away the danger, and she didn't claim any special promise that she would be safe. Her reasoning was simpler. The Waorani had asked her to come. She was one of the very few outsiders who had begun to learn their language. She believed God had called her to make Christ known to people who had never heard of him, and these were those people. She didn't think being a mother released her from obedience. And she didn't think obedience guaranteed a good outcome.

People have often told this as a dramatic act of forgiveness: a widow going to find her husband's killers so she could love them. She didn't describe it that way. She went as a missionary to a people. The fact that some of them had killed Jim was part of the situation, not the point of it. Forgiveness was real and necessary, but it wasn't a performance. It was simply the condition of going at all.

Early in October 1958 Elisabeth, Valerie and Rachel Saint walked into the forest with Dayuma and the Waorani who had come to fetch them. Valerie had to be carried. On 8 October, by the date usually given, they reached a clearing by a small river called the Tiwaeno. It would have been Jim's thirty-first birthday, and it was their fifth wedding anniversary.

The houses were big shelters thatched with palm leaves, with hammocks slung inside. People grew manioc and plantains, hunted monkeys and birds with blowguns and spears, and wore almost nothing. Most had never seen a foreigner up close, let alone a fair-haired little girl. Elisabeth and Valerie lived in a simple thatched shelter. The Waorani gave Elisabeth a name: Gikari, which means woodpecker. Valerie started picking up Waorani from the children she played with. Dayuma, home at last, began telling her people Bible stories in her own way.

Among the people of the clearing were men who had been on the beach. Gikita, who had led the attack, was there. So were Kimo, Dyuwi and Mincaye. Most of the men who had killed Jim were living a few yards from his widow and daughter.

What did she feel? She didn't claim to feel nothing, and she didn't claim to feel only love. What struck her again and again was how ordinary they were. They laughed, joked, argued, looked after their children, mourned their dead and went hunting. They had killed the five men, as they had killed many others, out of fear and anger and a long habit of violence, and in time they talked about it plainly. She didn't excuse it. She didn't pretend it didn't matter. But she didn't hate them. She had settled that before she came. Now she had to live it, every day, at their fires.

Overcoming evil with good is one of the hardest commands in the Bible. It doesn't mean pretending a wrong wasn't wrong. And here's something important: forgiving someone is not the same as putting yourself back where they can hurt you. Elisabeth went because she believed God was calling her and the people had invited her, not because forgiveness required it. If someone is still harming you, forgiveness can start with telling a safe adult what's happening.

One thing to do this week: think of one person you hold a grudge against. Pray for them by name every day this week, asking God to do them good, even if your feelings don't come along yet.

fields.title: Earthen Vessels
fields.body_html:
“But we have this treasure in earthen vessels, that the excellency of the power may be of God, and not of us.” — 2 Corinthians 4:7 (KJV)

Elisabeth lived among the Waorani for about three years, from October 1958 until late 1961. She shared the life of the clearing: its food, its weather, its illnesses and its quarrels. She handed out medicine, took photographs, filled notebooks, and kept working at the language. Valerie grew from a toddler into a little girl who ran barefoot with the Waorani children and spoke their language easily.

Something did change. Over the years, several people at Tiwaeno, including some of the men from the beach, began to call themselves followers of God. Gikita, Kimo, Dyuwi and Mincaye were among those who in time professed faith, and some became leaders among the believers. Dayuma's influence was crucial. The cycle of revenge killings began to slow among those living near the missionaries, though it didn't stop all at once, and other Waorani groups went on killing and being killed for years. A few years after Elisabeth left, Kimo and Dyuwi baptised two of Nate Saint's children, Steve and Kathy, in the Curaray River, near the beach where their father died.

In 1961 she published a book of photographs about her first year there. She called it The Savage My Kinsman. Readers who had soaked up newspaper talk of savages and martyrs were faced with pictures of ordinary men, women and children, and a title that insisted they were family. The book didn't claim mass conversions. It showed a people, and a missionary, at the start of a long road.

Living there was changing her. She was seeing how much of what she'd brought was American culture rather than the gospel, and how little she could be sure of about what the Waorani actually understood. She didn't lose her faith. But she was becoming less sure of many things the missionary movement at home took for granted.

The hardest part of Tiwaeno wasn't the forest or the Waorani. It was Rachel Saint. Both women loved the Waorani. Each had lost someone on the beach. But they were very different, and the differences proved impossible to bridge. Historians describe clashes of personality, theology, method and training. Rachel was older and intensely devoted, convinced God had given her a special calling to the Waorani through Dayuma; she came to treat the work, and to some extent the people, as hers. Elisabeth, the more highly trained linguist, wanted a careful analysis of the language and worried about how much the Waorani could really understand through a single go-between. They couldn't agree on translation, which was meant to be the centre of their work.

Neither woman comes out of it simply right. Rachel's possessiveness made life hard for Elisabeth. But Elisabeth could be cool, critical and quick to spot the weak points in other people's thinking, and she wasn't easy to work with either. Both were isolated, often ill, under huge pressure, and watched by Christians at home who expected a triumph.

Late in 1961 Elisabeth left Tiwaeno, without public complaint. Rachel stayed for most of the rest of her life. Elisabeth went back to the Quichua for about two more years, and in 1963 she and Valerie, now eight, returned to the United States. She had arrived in Ecuador in 1952 single, at twenty-five. She left at thirty-six, a widow with a daughter, the author of three books, and a far more questioning and seasoned Christian.

Paul calls the people who carry the gospel clay pots: cheap, breakable, sometimes cracked. That isn't a flaw in God's plan. It's the plan, so that everyone can see the power is God's and not ours. When Christians fight, it's ugly. But it doesn't mean God has stopped working. He has always worked through cracked pots, and that includes you.

One thing to do this week: if there is a conflict between you and someone at church, school or home, write down one way you have made it worse. Then do one thing to put that part right, whether or not they do their part.

fields.title: Pour Out Your Heart
fields.body_html:
“Trust in him at all times; ye people, pour out your heart before him: God is a refuge for us.” — Psalm 62:8 (KJV)

Back in America, Elisabeth and Valerie settled in Franconia, New Hampshire, where her family had spent its summers. She was famous. Churches, colleges and conferences wanted Jim Elliot's widow to come and tell the story, and since she now earned her living by writing and speaking, she accepted many invitations. But the woman who stood up to speak wasn't quite the woman audiences expected.

The story of 1956 had been told everywhere with a neat shape: five men died, and God used their deaths to open a closed people to the gospel. Elisabeth never denied that God had worked. She'd seen it. But she had also seen how much didn't fit the shape: a murdered helper, a stolen suitcase, a station washed away, rivalry among missionaries. She had hard questions about whether missionaries, herself included, understood what they were doing to a people's whole way of life, and how much of what they called the Lord's work was really their own plans in religious language. She decided the honest thing was to say so.

In 1966 she published a novel, No Graven Image. Its heroine is a young single missionary trying to put an unwritten language into writing in Ecuador, longing for a faithful helper and the success she's been taught to expect. Near the end, trying to help, she gives an injection to the very man her work depends on, and he dies. The novel doesn't turn it into a lesson. It ends with the missionary stripped of her assumptions about what God must do. Many readers who had loved her first book were dismayed. Some decided she had lost her faith. Others see it as the most searching thing she ever wrote. The title comes from the second commandment. A God who always has to produce the results we planned for him, she was saying, isn't the God of the Bible. He's an idol with a Christian name.

The biography is clear that this wasn't a woman abandoning Christ. Her letters and journals from those years show someone lonely and often unsure, but not walking away. What she abandoned was the habit of tidying things up. She came to believe a Christian's job is to trust God, not to explain him, and that the faithful thing to do with an unanswered question is to bring it to God rather than hide it.

Then her life changed again. In the later 1960s she met Addison Leitch, a Presbyterian theologian and teacher: big personality, funny, well read, and not at all overawed by her. His wife Margaret died in 1968 after a serious illness. Elisabeth and Addison were married on 1 January 1969. She was forty-two; he was sixty. They moved to Hamilton, Massachusetts, where he taught theology at a new seminary, Gordon-Conwell. Valerie gained a stepfather and four older stepsisters. By the accounts of those who knew them, the years with Addison were happy ones.

They didn't last. Addison was found to have cancer. Elisabeth nursed him at home and watched a large, vigorous man grow weak. He died on 17 September 1973 (a few accounts say the 18th). She was forty-six and a widow for the second time. This time there was no magazine spread and no book. She grieved without an audience. When she later wrote that suffering is never wasted, she wasn't writing from a desk. She had sat at a dying husband's bedside.

Psalm 62 doesn't tell you to tidy yourself up before you come to God. It says “pour out your heart before him,” because God is a refuge, and a refuge is for people in trouble. Honest questions aren't the opposite of faith. Hiding them is often more dangerous than asking them.

One thing to do this week: write God an honest prayer about a question you have been hiding, about him, about suffering, about something that happened to you. Don't clean it up. Then end it with one sentence of trust, even a small one.

study_questions.question: What is *No Graven Image* about, and why did it upset readers?
study_questions.answer: A young missionary whose efforts end with the death of the man her work depends on. Readers expecting another story of triumph found a missionary stripped of her assumptions about what God must do.

study_questions.question: Did Elisabeth lose her faith in the 1960s?
study_questions.answer: No. Her letters and journals show she was lonely and unsure but did not abandon Christ; she abandoned the habit of tidying up hard stories.

study_questions.question: How was her second widowhood different from her first?
study_questions.answer: The first was sudden, violent and public; the second came slowly through cancer, after months of nursing at home, and she grieved without an audience.

fields.title: Gateway to Joy
fields.body_html:
“The LORD hath appeared of old unto me, saying, Yea, I have loved thee with an everlasting love: therefore with lovingkindness have I drawn thee.” — Jeremiah 31:3 (KJV)

After Addison's death Elisabeth stayed in Hamilton, writing, speaking and teaching for a time at the seminary. One of the lodgers in her house was Lars Gren, ten years younger than her, a former salesman training to be a hospital chaplain. A friendship grew, then more. They married in December 1977. It was her third marriage. They later made their home in Magnolia, a village on the rocky Massachusetts coast. Lars ran the business side of her work: her diary, her travel, her book sales. He travelled with her almost everywhere, and her public work grew enormously.

Valerie grew up and married Walter Shepard, who became a Presbyterian minister. They had eight children. Around Valerie's wedding Elisabeth wrote her letters about being a woman, a wife and a Christian, published in 1976 as Let Me Be a Woman. She taught that the difference between men and women is God's gift, and that in marriage a wife is called to submit to her husband's headship. Many readers found dignity in it. Many Christians who love the Bible just as much disagreed sharply. They pointed out that she herself had gone alone into the forest and written down an unwritten language, and they warned that teaching submission without enough care could keep women in marriages that were harming them. Christians still debate it.

Her own marriage was harder than most readers knew. Our fullest account comes from her authorised biographer, Ellen Vaughn, writing after her death. Vaughn reports that Lars destroyed most of Elisabeth's journals from those years, something he came to regret. Drawing on family and close friends, she describes a husband given to outbursts of temper who came to control much of Elisabeth's daily life, including her diary and how often she saw her friends. Elisabeth never spoke of this in public. Lars's own side is largely missing from the record. And, as the next chapter shows, he was also the one who cared for her at home for years when her mind failed. Both are true.

Meanwhile her work reached more people than ever. From 1982 she sent out a plain newsletter. In 1984 came Passion and Purity, and in 1987 her life of Amy Carmichael, the missionary she'd first heard read aloud at fourteen. In 1988 a radio ministry in Lincoln, Nebraska, asked her to present a short daily programme for women. It was called Gateway to Joy, and it ran for thirteen years. Every programme opened the same way: reminding listeners that they were loved with an everlasting love, the words of Jeremiah 31:3, and that underneath were the everlasting arms, from Deuteronomy.

Then she talked about prayer, suffering, loneliness and widowhood, and also about washing dishes, being on time, answering letters and getting out of bed. She believed the Christian life is lived mostly in small things, and that doing small duties faithfully is not a lesser kind of devotion than dramatic sacrifice. She was crisp, direct and sometimes severe. Some found her cold. Many more, especially the lonely, the grieving and the worn out, found her bracing. She didn't tell them their troubles were small. She told them God was great and was with them.

There's a hard truth here. The woman who opened every programme with the everlasting arms was carrying burdens at home almost nobody suspected. People's public faces can hide a lot. That's true of people you admire, and maybe of you. If someone at home loses their temper in ways that frighten you, or controls who you can see and what you can do, that matters. Tell a safe person: a parent, a pastor, a teacher, a doctor, or a helpline where you live.

One thing to do this week: do one small, unnoticed duty without being asked, like the dishes, a tidy room, or a reply you've been putting off, and quietly offer it to God as worship.

study_questions.question: What was *Gateway to Joy*?
study_questions.answer: A short daily radio programme for women that Elisabeth presented for thirteen years, from 1988 to 2001, always opening with the reminder that listeners were loved with an everlasting love.

study_questions.question: Why was her teaching on men and women debated?
study_questions.answer: Many found it gave dignity to ordinary callings, but other Bible-believing Christians disagreed, noted that her own life broke the pattern, and warned that teaching submission without care could keep women in harmful marriages.

study_questions.question: What does the chapter say about her marriage to Lars Gren?
study_questions.answer: Her biographer Ellen Vaughn describes his temper and control of her daily life, though his own view is largely missing, and he also cared for her at home for years when she became ill. Both are part of the record.

fields.body_text: “The LORD hath appeared of old unto me, saying, Yea, I have loved thee with an everlasting love: therefore with lovingkindness have I drawn thee.” — Jeremiah 31:3 (KJV) After Addison's death Elisabeth stayed in Hamilton, writing, speaking and teaching for a time at the seminary. One of the lodgers in her house was Lars Gren, ten years younger than her, a former salesman training to be a hospital chaplain. A friendship grew, then more. They married in December 1977. It was her third marriage. They later made their home in Magnolia, a village on the rocky Massachusetts coast. Lars ran the business side of her work: her diary, her travel, her book sales. He travelled with her almost everywhere, and her public work grew enormously. Valerie grew up and married Walter Shepard, who became a Presbyterian minister. They had eight children. Around Valerie's wedding Elisabeth wrote her letters about being a woman, a wife and a Christian, published in 1976 as Let Me Be a Woman. She taught that the difference between men and women is God's gift, and that in marriage a wife is called to submit to her husband's headship. Many readers found dignity in it. Many Christians who love the Bible just as much disagreed sharply. They pointed out that she herself had gone alone into the forest and written down an unwritten language, and they warned that teaching submission without enough care could keep women in marriages that were harming them. Christians still debate it. Her own marriage was harder than most readers knew. Our fullest account comes from her authorised biographer, Ellen Vaughn, writing after her death. Vaughn reports that Lars destroyed most of Elisabeth's journals from those years, something he came to regret. Drawing on family and close friends, she describes a husband given to outbursts of temper who came to control much of Elisabeth's daily life, including her diary and how often she saw her friends. Elisabeth never spoke of this in public. Lars's own side is largely missing from the record. And, as the next chapter shows, he was also the one who cared for her at home for years when her mind failed. Both are true. Meanwhile her work reached more people than ever. From 1982 she sent out a plain newsletter. In 1984 came Passion and Purity, and in 1987 her life of Amy Carmichael, the missionary she'd first heard read aloud at fourteen. In 1988 a radio ministry in Lincoln, Nebraska, asked her to present a short daily programme for women. It was called Gateway to Joy, and it ran for thirteen years. Every programme opened the same way: reminding listeners that they were loved with an everlasting love, the words of Jeremiah 31:3, and that underneath were the everlasting arms, from Deuteronomy. Then she talked about prayer, suffering, loneliness and widowhood, and also about washing dishes, being on time, answering letters and getting out of bed. She believed the Christian life is lived mostly in small things, and that doing small duties faithfully is not a lesser kind of devotion than dramatic sacrifice. She was crisp, direct and sometimes severe. Some found her cold. Many more, especially the lonely, the grieving and the worn out, found her bracing. She didn't tell them their troubles were small. She told them God was great and was with them. There's a hard truth here. The woman who opened every programme with the everlasting arms was carrying burdens at home almost nobody suspected. People's public faces can hide a lot. That's true of people you admire, and maybe of you. If someone at home loses their temper in ways that frighten you, or controls who you can see and what you can do, that matters. Tell a safe person: a parent, a pastor, a teacher, a doctor, or a helpline where you live. One thing to do this week: do one small, unnoticed duty without being asked, like the dishes, a tidy room, or a reply you've been putting off, and quietly offer it to God as worship.

fields.title: Carried
fields.body_html:
“And even to your old age I am he; and even to hoar hairs will I carry you: I have made, and I will bear; even I will carry, and will deliver you.” — Isaiah 46:4 (KJV)

In 1996, forty years after Palm Beach, a new edition of Through Gates of Splendor came out. Elisabeth added an epilogue admitting plainly that events among the Waorani hadn't unfolded as simply as the first telling, and many sermons since, suggested. Killings didn't stop at once. The church grew, but unevenly. Relations between outsiders and the Waorani had been more tangled and more painful than people liked to think. It wasn't a retraction. She still believed God had been at work and that the five men had been right to go. But she would not let the story harden into a legend. Her reputation would have been safer if she had left it alone. She didn't.

She had lived by words: Greek at Wheaton, Spanish, Colorado, Quichua, Waorani, more than twenty books, hundreds of radio talks. And it was her words that began to go first. In the late 1990s her family noticed lapses of memory and moments of confusion. By about 2000 she had been diagnosed with dementia. Gateway to Joy ended in 2001, the newsletter in 2003, and in 2004 she gave up speaking. After that she simply disappeared from public life.

Some people asked how a woman who had taught so many to trust God in suffering could be brought to a place where she couldn't speak of him at all. She had no answer to give them now. But she had given it long before: God doesn't owe us an explanation, and nothing offered to him is wasted. In her last years she couldn't say that anymore. She could only live it.

Lars decided she would stay at home. Instead of placing her in a nursing home, he cared for her himself in the house at Magnolia for the rest of her life, the better part of fifteen years, and in the end around the clock. Whatever else is true of their marriage, this was faithful service, and it deserves to be remembered. Valerie and her family visited. Old friends came when they could.

Elisabeth Elliot died at home on the morning of 15 June 2015, aged eighty-eight. Her funeral was at Gordon College, near where she had spent the second half of her life, and a memorial service was held at Wheaton, where she had studied Greek seventy years before.

Her books are still in print. Honest biographies have shown her as proud at times, often lonely, sometimes harsh, and capable of real mistakes, and somehow that has made her more believable, not less. The story of 1956 has been retold with the Waorani's own voices: Dayuma, Mintaka and Mankamu, and the men who chose to put down the spear. Mincaye, one of the men from the beach, became a close friend of Nate Saint's son Steve and travelled with him telling his own story. In a way Elisabeth started that, by refusing to let the first telling be the last.

Isaiah contrasts God with idols that have to be loaded onto animals and carried around. The true God does the opposite: he carries his people, all the way to grey hair. Elisabeth spent her life carrying others: a baby in the jungle, a dying husband, a story the whole world wanted told, and millions of readers' sorrows. At the end she could carry nothing, not even her own memories. Someone else carried her, and behind every human hand, God did. Your worth isn't measured by what you can do. A life that can do almost nothing is still precious to him.

One thing to do this week: visit, call or write to an elderly person, a grandparent, a neighbour, someone in a care home, and spend real time with them. If you know someone who looks after a sick or elderly relative, thank them.
